items.stem: Which term describes a process of economic, social and political change that improves people’s living standards and life chances?
items.answer: Development
items.markingKey: Development: a process of economic, social and political change that improves people’s living standards and life chances. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Human Development Index”? Give one example.
items.answer: A UN measure combining life expectancy, education and income per head. Example: a country with an HDI of 0.85.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a UN measure combining life expectancy, education and income per head); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a country with an HDI of 0.85. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “multidimensional poverty” and “Sustainable Development Goals”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Multidimensional poverty: poverty measured by several deprivations, such as health, education and living standards, not income alone (e.g. lacking clean water, schooling and electricity). Sustainable Development Goals: UN targets agreed in 2015 to reduce poverty, inequality and environmental damage by 2030 (e.g. a goal to end extreme poverty).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Country X has a higher GNI per capita than Country Y, but lower life expectancy and literacy rates. Suggest how a world-systems sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: World-systems theory: the world is a single capitalist system of core, semi-periphery and periphery; countries can move between positions, but the system keeps inequality (Wallerstein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Country X has a higher GNI per capita than Country Y, but lower life expectancy and literacy rates. Explain how a dependency sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Dependency theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because they were exploited by colonialism and remain dependent on richer countries through trade, debt and TNCs; the core develops at the expense of the periphery (Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research changes in development indicators over thirty years.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in development indicators over thirty years but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “development”?
items.answer: A process of economic, social and political change that improves people’s living standards and life chances.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a process of economic, social and political change that improves people’s living standards and life chances. [1]

items.stem: A research team is investigating changes in development indicators over thirty years. Explain one strength of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of changes in development indicators over thirty years. [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the theory that poorer countries can develop by adopting Western values, institutions, technology and investment?
items.answer: Modernisation theory
items.markingKey: Modernisation theory: the theory that poorer countries can develop by adopting Western values, institutions, technology and investment. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “trickle-down”, and give one example.
items.answer: The idea that the benefits of economic growth will eventually spread to the poor. Example: new factory jobs raising incomes across a region.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the idea that the benefits of economic growth will eventually spread to the poor); 1 mark for a relevant example such as new factory jobs raising incomes across a region. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “stages of economic growth” and “modernisation theory”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Stages of economic growth: Rostow’s five stages through which he believed all societies pass on the way to mass consumption (e.g. traditional society, preconditions, take-off, drive to maturity, mass consumption). Modernisation theory: the theory that poorer countries can develop by adopting Western values, institutions, technology and investment (e.g. a country building factories with Western aid).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A village near Mumbai receives high-yield seeds and fertiliser through an aid programme; harvests increase but poorer farmers fall into debt. Suggest how a dependency sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Dependency theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because they were exploited by colonialism and remain dependent on richer countries through trade, debt and TNCs; the core develops at the expense of the periphery (Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A government near Bangkok invites Western companies to build factories and sends students abroad to study engineering, hoping to “catch up” with rich countries. Explain how a post-development sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Post-development theory: the Western idea of development is itself a problem: it imposes Western values and ignores local knowledge, so communities should define their own goals (Escobar, Sachs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A government near Lima invites Western companies to build factories and sends students abroad to study engineering, hoping to “catch up” with rich countries. Explain how post-development and neoliberal sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Post-development theory: the Western idea of development is itself a problem: it imposes Western values and ignores local knowledge, so communities should define their own goals (Escobar, Sachs). Neoliberalism: development comes from free markets, free trade, privatisation and reduced state spending; aid and state intervention distort markets (structural adjustment, IMF and World Bank).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying the effects of foreign aid on a rural community.
items.answer: Strengths: they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of foreign aid on a rural community but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of attitudes to “modern” and “traditional” values. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying attitudes to “modern” and “traditional” values but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes values such as fatalism, collectivism and ascribed status, which modernisation theorists saw as barriers to development?
items.answer: Traditional values
items.markingKey: Traditional values: values such as fatalism, collectivism and ascribed status, which modernisation theorists saw as barriers to development. [1]

items.stem: Assess how useful structured interviews are for studying the effects of foreign aid on a rural community.
items.answer: Strengths: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of foreign aid on a rural community but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the theory that poorer countries are underdeveloped because they have been exploited by richer countries through colonialism and unequal trade?
items.answer: Dependency theory
items.markingKey: Dependency theory: the theory that poorer countries are underdeveloped because they have been exploited by richer countries through colonialism and unequal trade. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “core, semi-periphery and periphery”, and give one example.
items.answer: Wallerstein’s three zones of the capitalist world system. Example: rich industrial core, middle-income semi-periphery, poor periphery.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Wallerstein’s three zones of the capitalist world system); 1 mark for a relevant example such as rich industrial core, middle-income semi-periphery, poor periphery. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “unequal exchange” and “cash crop”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Unequal exchange: trade in which poorer countries export low-value primary goods and import high-value manufactured goods (e.g. exporting coffee beans and importing machinery). Cash crop: a crop grown for export rather than for local consumption (e.g. cocoa or coffee grown for world markets).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A country that was poor in 1960 now produces cars and electronics and has incomes close to those of Western Europe. Suggest how a world-systems sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: World-systems theory: the world is a single capitalist system of core, semi-periphery and periphery; countries can move between positions, but the system keeps inequality (Wallerstein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A former colony near Colombo still earns 70% of its export income from coffee, whose world price has fallen by a third in five years. Explain how a world-systems sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: World-systems theory: the world is a single capitalist system of core, semi-periphery and periphery; countries can move between positions, but the system keeps inequality (Wallerstein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A former colony near Nairobi still earns 70% of its export income from coffee, whose world price has fallen by a third in five years. Explain how modernisation and dependency sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Modernisation theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because of traditional values and institutions; they can develop by adopting Western values, investment, education and industrialisation, passing through stages of growth (Rostow, Parsons). Dependency theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because they were exploited by colonialism and remain dependent on richer countries through trade, debt and TNCs; the core develops at the expense of the periphery (Frank).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating trade between rich and poor countries. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; positivists see them as objective “social facts” that can be used to test hypotheses. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying trade between rich and poor countries but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research trade between rich and poor countries.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; comparing the same people at different points avoids the problem of comparing different samples. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying trade between rich and poor countries but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “neo-colonialism”?
items.answer: Continued control of poorer countries by richer ones through economic means such as trade, debt and TNCs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: continued control of poorer countries by richer ones through economic means such as trade, debt and TNCs. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “core, semi-periphery and periphery” and “unequal exchange”?
items.answer: Core, semi-periphery and periphery: Wallerstein’s three zones of the capitalist world system. Unequal exchange: trade in which poorer countries export low-value primary goods and import high-value manufactured goods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that development comes from free markets, free trade, privatisation and a limited role for the state?
items.answer: Neoliberalism
items.markingKey: Neoliberalism: the view that development comes from free markets, free trade, privatisation and a limited role for the state. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “grassroots development”, and give one example.
items.answer: Development projects led by local communities rather than governments or foreign agencies. Example: a women’s cooperative running a village water project.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (development projects led by local communities rather than governments or foreign agencies); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a women’s cooperative running a village water project. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “post-development theory” and “structural adjustment programmes”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Post-development theory: the view that the idea of development itself is a Western project that should be replaced by locally defined alternatives (e.g. communities rejecting large dams in favour of local projects). Structural adjustment programmes: conditions imposed by the IMF and World Bank on loans, such as cutting public spending and opening markets (e.g. a country cutting food subsidies to receive a loan).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.answer: Post-development theory: the Western idea of development is itself a problem: it imposes Western values and ignores local knowledge, so communities should define their own goals (Escobar, Sachs).

items.stem: Chloe is planning a study of the effects of privatisation of water services. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect; they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory. Limitations: participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of privatisation of water services but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A community near Colombo rejects a large dam funded by international lenders and instead builds small irrigation schemes managed by local farmers. Suggest how a post-development sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Post-development theory: the Western idea of development is itself a problem: it imposes Western values and ignores local knowledge, so communities should define their own goals (Escobar, Sachs).

items.stem: Which term describes the total income of a country divided by its population, used as a measure of average income?
items.answer: Gross national income per capita
items.markingKey: Gross national income per capita: the total income of a country divided by its population, used as a measure of average income. [1]

items.stem: Rostow argued that societies develop through five stages of economic growth. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Rostow’s stages run from traditional society through take-off to the age of high mass consumption. Criticism: Dependency theorists argue it ignores exploitation and history.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Modernisation theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows life expectancy in three countries, from official international data. Table: life expectancy at birth (years) | 1990 | 2020. Country A | 45 | 53. Country B | 65 | 75. Country C | 73 | 76. By how many years did the figure for Country B change between 1990 and 2020?
items.answer: +10 years

items.stem: The table shows life expectancy in three countries, from official international data. Table: life expectancy at birth (years) | 1990 | 2020. Country A | 45 | 63. Country B | 55 | 66. Country C | 75 | 78. (a) Calculate the change, in years, for Country A between 1990 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that development is improving people’s lives in poorer countries.
items.answer: (a) 63 − 45 = +18 years. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country C had the highest figure for 2020. Rising incomes and education. Qualifications: Gaps remain large; averages hide inequality within countries; life expectancy is one indicator only; data quality may vary. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 45 and 63; 1 mark for +18 years (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Green Revolution”?
items.answer: The use of new high-yield seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to increase food production in developing countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the use of new high-yield seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to increase food production in developing countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “Green Revolution” and “trickle-down”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Green Revolution: the use of new high-yield seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to increase food production in developing countries (e.g. India’s wheat yields rising in the 1960s). Trickle-down: the idea that the benefits of economic growth will eventually spread to the poor (e.g. new factory jobs raising incomes across a region).

items.answer: Open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning.

items.stem: Nadia is planning a study of attitudes to “modern” and “traditional” values. Explain two limitations of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. The researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it. 2. The presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect).
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to attitudes to “modern” and “traditional” values. [4]

items.stem: (a) Explain two ways in which modernisation theorists argue that poorer countries can develop. (b) Evaluate the view that modernisation theory provides an adequate explanation of development.
items.answer: (a) Adopting modern values; Western aid and investment; education and mass media; industrialisation; urbanisation; stages of growth. (b) For: Success of East Asian economies; role of investment, education and technology; the Green Revolution increased food output. Against: Dependency theory (Frank): exploitation; ethnocentrism; aid benefits elites; environmental damage; post-development critique; neoliberal emphasis on markets instead of aid. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.

Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Adopting modern values; Western aid and investment; education and mass media; industrialisation; urbanisation; stages of growth. [8] (b) Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. items.stem: International trade data for three commodity-exporting countries are shown below. Table: main export as a percentage of total export earnings | 2000 | 2020. Country A (coffee) | 69% | 68%. Country B (copper) | 68% | 72%. Country C (cocoa) | 46% | 48%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country B (copper) between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Country B (copper) and Country C (cocoa) in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) (72 − 68) ÷ 68 × 100 = 5.9%. (b) 2000: 22 percentage points; 2020: 24 percentage points; the gap widened.

items.stem: Assess how useful semi-structured interviews are for studying living standards in rural communities in the Global South.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; the interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity. Limitations: samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited; interviewer bias may still affect answers. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying living standards in rural communities in the Global South but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes Rostow’s five stages through which he believed all societies pass on the way to mass consumption?
items.answer: Stages of economic growth
items.markingKey: Stages of economic growth: Rostow’s five stages through which he believed all societies pass on the way to mass consumption. [1]

items.stem: State one role that modernisation theorists give to the West in development.
items.answer: Providing aid to fund investment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. providing aid to fund investment. [1]

items.stem: Explain Parsons’s argument that traditional values such as particularism and ascribed status are barriers to development, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Parsons argued that development requires a shift to universalistic values, achieved status and individualism. Criticism: This is ethnocentric, treating Western values as superior.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Modernisation theory); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A village near Toronto receives high-yield seeds and fertiliser through an aid programme; harvests increase but poorer farmers fall into debt. Suggest how a dependency sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Dependency theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because they were exploited by colonialism and remain dependent on richer countries through trade, debt and TNCs; the core develops at the expense of the periphery (Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A village near Santiago receives high-yield seeds and fertiliser through an aid programme; harvests increase but poorer farmers fall into debt. Explain how a neoliberal sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: development comes from free markets, free trade, privatisation and reduced state spending; aid and state intervention distort markets (structural adjustment, IMF and World Bank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the effects of foreign aid on a rural community. Evaluate the use of semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of foreign aid on a rural community but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes Frank’s terms for rich, dominant countries and poorer countries that are exploited by them?
items.answer: Metropolis and satellite
items.markingKey: Metropolis and satellite: Frank’s terms for rich, dominant countries and poorer countries that are exploited by them. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Dependency theory sees traditional values as the main cause of underdevelopment.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. That is modernisation theory; dependency theory blames exploitation by richer countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: A country that was poor in 1960 now produces cars and electronics and has incomes close to those of Western Europe. Suggest how a modernisation sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Modernisation theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because of traditional values and institutions; they can develop by adopting Western values, investment, education and industrialisation, passing through stages of growth (Rostow, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: International trade data for three commodity-exporting countries are shown below. Table: main export as a percentage of total export earnings | 2000 | 2020. Country A (coffee) | 65% | 70%. Country B (copper) | 63% | 73%. Country C (cocoa) | 58% | 55%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country A (coffee) between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Country A (coffee) and Country B (copper) in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) (70 − 65) ÷ 65 × 100 = 7.7%. (b) 2000: 2 percentage points; 2020: 3 percentage points; the gap widened.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (70 − 65) ÷ 65 × 100; 1 mark for 7.7% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (2 and 3); 1 mark for “widened”. [3]

items.stem: A country that was poor in 1960 now produces cars and electronics and has incomes close to those of Western Europe. Explain how a dependency sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Dependency theory: poorer countries are underdeveloped because they were exploited by colonialism and remain dependent on richer countries through trade, debt and TNCs; the core develops at the expense of the periphery (Frank).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: International trade data for three commodity-exporting countries are shown below. Table: main export as a percentage of total export earnings | 2000 | 2020. Country A (coffee) | 56% | 54%. Country B (copper) | 61% | 56%. Country C (cocoa) | 47% | 52%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country C (cocoa) between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of commodity dependence. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that poorer countries remain dependent on richer countries.
items.answer: (a) (52 − 47) ÷ 47 × 100 = 10.6%. (b) Definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country C (cocoa); the figure fell for Country A (coffee), Country B (copper); Country B (copper) had the highest figure for 2020. Lack of investment in manufacturing. Qualifications: Some countries have diversified; internal factors such as governance matter; dependence may reflect comparative advantage, as neoliberals argue. The data also come from official statistics of 3 countries in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (52 − 47) ÷ 47 × 100; 1 mark for 10.6% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: State one criticism of structural adjustment programmes.
items.answer: Privatisation sold assets cheaply to foreign companies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. privatisation sold assets cheaply to foreign companies. [1]

items.stem: Explain two features of the neoliberal approach to development.
items.answer: Free markets and trade; privatisation; reduced state spending and deregulation; foreign investment; structural adjustment conditions on loans; aid seen as distorting markets.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained feature. [4]

items.stem: A community near Hanoi rejects a large dam funded by international lenders and instead builds small irrigation schemes managed by local farmers. Suggest how a post-development sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Post-development theory: the Western idea of development is itself a problem: it imposes Western values and ignores local knowledge, so communities should define their own goals (Escobar, Sachs).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research grassroots development projects led by women.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewee can raise issues the researcher had not thought of, so the research is not limited by pre-set categories. Limitations: each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying grassroots development projects led by women but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
